study type: Secondary analysis of demographic and health surveys and multiple indicator cluster surveys
exposure: Five subgroups of household wealth status (poorest to richest fifth)
outcome: Absolute inequality in cesarean section rates
Relative inequality in cesarean section rates
Change in cesarean section rates over time
cohort: Women aged 15-49 years with a live birth during the two or three years preceding the survey in 72 low and middle-income countries
finding: Substantial economic inequalities in cesarean deliveries persist within countries, with higher rates among the richest compared to the poorest, potentially reflecting disparities in access to emergency obstetric care and overuse of cesarean sections without medical indication.
